author: simon-lea
description: In 1513, Niccolò Machiavelli, tortured and then exiled by the new masters of Florence, wrote a short handbook of power for the prince who had wrecked his career. He never got the job he hoped for, but his book founded modern political thought.

hero.hook: A man tortured by the Medici wrote them a handbook of power, hoping they would give him his job back.

blocks.text: In **1512**, the powerful [[Medici]] family returned to power in Florence. Those who had served the previous regime were dealt with harshly. [[Niccolò Machiavelli]], an official of middling rank, was no exception. In **February 1513** he was arrested and tortured, then chose exile on the family farm, a few kilometers outside the city.

His body broken, his career over and poverty looming, he had to act. Machiavelli wanted his old position back, even under new masters. His plan was audacious. Ten months into his exile, he sat down to write *The Prince*, a short text with a single aim: persuading [[Lorenzo II de' Medici]], the very man who had him arrested and tortured, to give him a job.

The contents of *The Prince* were shockingly new. Machiavelli says bluntly that to achieve greatness, a prince must be cruel and deceitful. The idea itself was nothing new: everybody knew that successful leaders used deception and were often cruel. What was startlingly original was to present these faults as virtues, and to put them down in black and white.

blocks.caption: Binding by Jean Picard for the bibliophile Jean Grolier on a copy of The Prince, 16th century.

blocks.text: Machiavelli never saw his book in print. Written in 1513, *The Prince* was first published in 1532, five years after his death.

To understand why he hoped the book would win him favor and a job, we need to know what kind of book it is. *The Prince* is a [[mirror for princes]]: a guidebook written by an expert and given to a ruler to show him how to achieve greatness. By offering it to Lorenzo, Machiavelli was saying two things: he wanted Lorenzo to be great, a display of loyalty, and he was willing to help him get there, a display of usefulness.

*The Prince* opens with a letter addressed to Lorenzo de' Medici. In it, Machiavelli expresses the hope that the lessons in the book will help bring him greatness. He signs off by claiming to have been unfairly treated, and by directly asking for generosity. Put simply, Machiavelli is asking for a job.

blocks.caption: Lorenzo the Magnificent, grandfather of the man The Prince is dedicated to, in a portrait by Peter Paul Rubens.

blocks.text: Experts remain divided over what the gesture means. Was Machiavelli flattering Lorenzo in the hope of a reward, or diplomatically criticizing him? In other words, was Lorenzo meant to recognize himself in the leader described, or to read in it what he could become? If the latter, the message would be: if you want to hold on to power, I am the man you need as a trusted advisor.

The most notorious of the **26** short chapters of *The Prince* is the eighteenth, "A Ruler and His Promises." Machiavelli argues there that while every leader must be seen as just and virtuous, the truly great ones are willing to lie and break their promises whenever their ends require it.

He draws on well-known fables from antiquity, in which the lion stands for force and the fox for cunning. Accepted wisdom held that a good leader charts a course between the two: neither a lion, who makes people obey through violence, nor a fox, who gets everything through deceit. Machiavelli turns the rule on its head: rather than avoiding being lion or fox, Lorenzo ought to become both lion **and** fox. Cruel and cunning, then.

The plan failed: Lorenzo never offered Machiavelli a job. But *The Prince* became one of the founding books of political philosophy. Its ideas and the difficult questions it raises proved indispensable to anyone seeking to lead in the 16th century, and they remain so today.

blocks.caption: Machiavelli's cenotaph in the basilica of Santa Croce, Florence (1787). The epitaph reads: "No praise is equal to so great a name."

blocks.text: The book touches on three issues in modern political theory: [[realpolitik]], the problem of [[dirty hands]] and the idea that the ends justify the means. When experts discuss politics, they often reason in terms of ideals. Machiavelli is interested only in results. His text argues for putting circumstances before ideology, and for making hard decisions for the greater good.

His ideas are certainly not accepted without question. Yet they remain a powerful presence in political thinking today. Five centuries after this little book written to get a job back, the shadow of Machiavelli still looms over our most difficult political dilemmas.
Written in 1513 by an exile who wanted a position back under the Medici, *The Prince* missed its immediate target and founded modern political thought.
